lessons.title: Travelling in the Past

activities.prompt: How did people journey through the world long ago?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways People Travelled
activities.body: Transport means the ways people travel from place to place. People have always been interested in travelling. Vehicles are things used for travel, such as carts, cars, trains, boats, and ships. In earlier years, there were far fewer vehicles. Long before that, people travelled on foot or used animals. Boats were probably the first transport invented by humans.
keyPoints: People have always been interested in travelling.
People travelled on foot, with animals, and by vehicle.
Boats were probably the first kind of transport invented by humans.
activities.explanation: These are the main travel methods from the lesson.

Therefore, 8 animals are needed for the two carts.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing Large Numbers

activities.prompt: How can commas make really big numbers easier to read?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The TTh Column
activities.body: The place value chart now has a TTh column. TTh stands for ten thousand. Ten Ones make one Ten. Ten Tens make one Hundred. Ten Hundreds make one Thousand. Ten Thousands make Ten Thousand. A comma helps us read large numbers easily. Numbers beyond 10,000 are written like numbers below 9,999. The number 9,123 has 9 Thousands, 1 Hundred, 2 Tens, and 3 Ones.
keyPoints: TTh means ten thousand.
A comma helps us read large numbers.
Large numbers use place value columns.
activities.explanation: TTh means ten thousand.

activities.title: Compare, Swap, and Round
activities.body: The lesson shows how to compare numbers, swap digits, and round to the nearest ten. A student claimed that 9,990 was greater than 49,014 because 9 was greater than 4. A place value chart can help compare numbers. Interchanging 7 and 4 in 1,478 gives 1,748. The nearest ten of 2,346 is 2,350. Also, 19 and 21 both have nearest ten 20.
keyPoints: A place value chart can help compare numbers.
Interchanging 7 and 4 in 1,478 gives 1,748.
The nearest ten of 2,346 is 2,350.
activities.explanation: Careful comparisons and rounding give clearer results.

activities.prompt: Two card piles have 9,990 and 49,014 cards. Which pile has more cards, and why?
steps: Start with the thousands place, because it shows the bigger place.

49,014 has more thousands, so it has more cards.

activities.title: Rounding Around the Rabbit
activities.body: The rabbit needs 4 jumps to reach 2,350. Its food for the nearest-hundred activity is at a neighbouring hundred. Its food for the nearest-thousand activity is at a neighbouring thousand. These clues give examples of rounding to hundreds and thousands. Vijay and Suma got the same rounding result, so their rounded answers matched.

Nearest-hundred food is at a neighbouring hundred.
Nearest-thousand food is at a neighbouring thousand.

lessons.title: Travelling Now and Then

activities.prompt: How has the way people travel changed through the years?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways of travelling
activities.body: Long ago, travellers used animals for journeys. Bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules and elephants helped them travel. Camels were used in deserts. Today, people use bicycles, motorbikes, cars, buses, trains, ships and aeroplanes. Submarines travel deep underwater, while spacecraft carry people into outer space. Different journeys cover very different distances each hour.
keyPoints: Past travellers used animals, including bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules and elephants.
Camels were used in deserts.
Modern travel includes trains, ships and aeroplanes.
Submarines go under water, and spacecraft carry people to outer space.
activities.explanation: This lesson compares old and new ways to travel.

activities.context: The king was fond of his 20 horses in the royal stable, where a caretaker cared for them. During the night, a thief stole one horse. Fearing punishment, the caretaker rearranged the horses. The king counted 5 horses along each side, and the caretaker’s count gave a total of 20 horses. The king returned to his palace after hearing the explanation. After another theft, 18 horses remained, and the caretaker arranged them with 5 horses on each side.
activities.prompt: Why did the caretaker rearrange the horses after the first theft?
options: To keep the king’s count from revealing the missing horse.
To show the king that the horses needed different care.
To make the royal stable easier for the horses to move.
To let the king see every horse at the same time.

why.To show the king that the horses needed: The case mentions no problem with the horses’ care.
why.To make the royal stable easier for the: His reason was fear of punishment, not difficulty moving.
why.To let the king see every horse at the s: The arrangement supported the count of 20; it was not for displaying every horse.

activities.explanation: He feared punishment and used the arrangement to support his total.

why.The thief can keep taking horses without: Nothing says that stealing can continue without limit.
why.The caretaker will confess before anothe: Nothing says that the caretaker intends to confess.

activities.explanation: No stated rule explains exactly when the king will notice.

activities.prompt: Explain why the caretaker rearranged the horses after the first theft.
activities.answer: The caretaker rearranged the horses because he feared punishment after one was stolen. By arranging them with 5 along each side, he supported his count of 20. The king believed the explanation and returned to his palace. The rearrangement therefore helped hide the fact that a horse was missing.

The caretaker feared punishment.
He arranged 5 horses along each side.
The king accepted the explanation and returned to his palace.

activities.title: Fair fractions
activities.body: Two fractions can be compared when their wholes are the same size. Picture each whole using equal pieces of the same size. You can then compare the shaded parts fairly. activities.title: Different names for the same part
activities.body: Sameer shades one-third of several figures. He uses horizontal lines to divide the figures into more equal parts. The shaded region can stay the same while its fraction gets a different name. One-third, two-sixths and three-ninths can show the same shaded part. Equivalent fractions show the same part of a whole under different names.

Equivalent fractions name the same shaded region.

3 x 4 = 12, so the whole has 12 equal parts.

lessons.title: Full, Half and Everyday Turns

activities.title: Understanding Full and Half Turns
activities.body: A full turn makes a complete circle. A half turn can make a half-moon shape. The minute hand returns to its initial position after a full turn. A giant wheel makes a full turn when it returns to its starting position. Many everyday objects involve turns. Angles arise in situations that involve a turn.
keyPoints: A full turn makes a complete circle.
A half turn can make a half-moon shape.
Turns are involved in many everyday situations.
activities.explanation: Turns can be seen in clocks, wheels, objects and many daily activities.

activities.title: Turns and Angles
activities.body: A quarter of a full turn looks like a right angle. A turn smaller than a quarter turn looks acute. A turn larger than a quarter but smaller than a half looks obtuse. Two quarter turns make a straight angle. A paper fan can show different acute and obtuse angles. You can see its turns while keeping one side fixed.
keyPoints: A quarter turn looks like a right angle.
Smaller turns look acute.
Larger turns can look obtuse.
Two quarter turns make a straight angle.
activities.explanation: This lesson helps you name angles from the size of a turn.

activities.prompt: A bus makes 16 quarter turns in the same direction. How many full turns is that?
steps: The bus makes 16 quarter turns.
Four quarter turns make one full turn, so share 16 quarter turns into groups of four.
16 ÷ 4 = 4 full turns.

Turns over a quarter look obtuse because they stay under a half.
So the fan can show different acute and obtuse angles.

activities.title: Checking Related Amounts
activities.body: Addition and subtraction have a relationship. An equation shows that two amounts are equal. The minibus had 18 litres before refuelling and 65 litres after. lessons.title: Quick Sums, Palindromes and Even or Odd

activities.prompt: Can you discover quick tricks and secret patterns hiding in today’s numbers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Quick Sums and Palindromes
activities.body: Piku shows an interesting way to solve sums. Adding 32 and 68 gives 100. Sukanta likes 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000, while Namita likes 9. Namita also likes subtracting 9 or 99. A palindrome number reads the same from left to right and right to left. Examples are 22, 363, 404 and 8,558. The pairs 12 and 6 are even, while 13 and 9 are odd.
keyPoints: Palindromes read the same both ways.
Some pairs are even, while others are odd.
activities.explanation: These examples help you check sums, palindromes, even pairs and odd pairs.

activities.prompt: Piku has 12 and 22. Which card should join a palindrome group?

Change the fuel plan first, because interchanging the cards cannot affect the sums.

activities.title: Choosing the Right Unit
activities.body: Choose suitable units when you measure length. The India Gate is 42 metres high. A handkerchief is 40 centimetres long. A well is 50 metres deep. A mobile phone is 13 centimetres long. An elephant’s trunk is 2 metres long. The gap between shirt buttons is 5 centimetres. Different units have relationships. The double number line helps match measures for the same sari or stole.
keyPoints: Metres and centimetres are units for length, and they have relationships.
The lesson gives measures for objects such as India Gate and a handkerchief.
The double number line matches measures for the same sari or stole.
activities.explanation: These examples help you choose the right unit and practise matching.

100 - 60 = 40 centimetres.

activities.prompt: How can we discover how far away places are?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways to Measure Long Distances
activities.body: Long distances can be measured in several ways. The listed tools are Long Tape, Rangefinder, Rodometer and Laser Distance Meter. On the school playground, we can measure 100 m and 200 m. We mark these points and draw a straight line. Then we walk on the line and count our steps. The kilometre measures long distances, and kilo means thousand.
keyPoints: Several tools can measure long distances.
We can measure 100 m and 200 m on the school playground.
The kilometre measures long distances, and kilo means thousand.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect tools, steps, metres and kilometres.

activities.prompt: A child walks 20 metres along a straight line and takes 4 steps for each metre. How many steps does the child take in total?
steps: The distance walked is 20 metres.
There are 4 steps for each metre, so multiply the distance by 4.
20 x 4 = 80 steps.

activities.prompt: How can I measure long distances around my home?
steps: On the school playground, I can measure 100 m and 200 m, so I can set known distances.
I can mark these points and draw a straight line, because this gives me a clear path to walk.
I can walk on the line and count my steps, because step count is related to distance walked.
I can do this for at least three places near home, so I can compare distances and find the nearest and farthest places.

activities.title: Steps Help Us Compare Distances
activities.body: Marking points and drawing a straight line helps us measure distances on the playground. We walk on the line and count the number of steps. The number of steps is related to the distance walked. This relationship helps us find distances around us for at least three locations. We can then ask which locations are nearest to and farthest from home.
keyPoints: We count steps after marking points and drawing a line.
The number of steps is related to the distance walked.
The activity asks for locations nearest to and farthest from home.
activities.explanation: Counting steps helps us compare distances around us.

activities.title: Meet the Millimetre
activities.body: A centimetre is divided into ten equal parts. Each part is one millimetre, a unit for measuring smaller lengths. So, one centimetre equals ten millimetres. Small marks help us measure smaller lengths more precisely. One hundred centimetres equal one metre.

Each equal part is one millimetre.
One hundred centimetres equal one metre.

activities.prompt: Can regular shapes cover a surface without leaving any gaps?

activities.title: What is tessellation?
activities.body: Tessellation means tiles cover a region without gaps. Tiles may have same or different shapes. A pentagon has five sides. If all sides are equal, it is a regular pentagon. Regular pentagons leave gaps, so they do not tessellate. Regular triangles fit around a point without gaps or overlaps. Equilateral triangles tessellate. A tessellating pattern may use different shapes. Regular octagons have eight equal sides but do not tessellate.
keyPoints: Regular pentagons leave gaps.
Equilateral triangles tessellate.
Tessellations may use different shapes.

activities.title: Making a Circle Design
activities.body: First, draw a circle with a compass and mark its centre. A diameter has two marked endpoints. Draw another diameter and mark its endpoints too. Join the four marked points to make a circle design. The design can also use points marked from 1 to 24. Join them in the pattern 1 to 11, 11 to 2, and 2 to 12. Different coloured threads can be used.
keyPoints: Use a compass to draw the circle and mark its centre.
Mark the two endpoints of each diameter.
Join the four marked points.
Points from 1 to 24 can form a patterned design.
Different coloured threads can be used.
activities.explanation: Each step adds a mark before the final join.

activities.prompt: A circle design uses 4 diameters, and the two endpoints of each diameter are marked. How many marked endpoints are there?
steps: Each diameter has 2 marked endpoints.
Count the endpoints on all the diameters: 4 x 2 = 8.
The answer is 8 marked endpoints.

activities.title: Connecting cubes and solid shapes
activities.body: Big cube frames have small cubes removed. Nisha joins 27 small cubes into a large cube and paints it red. The cubes are sorted by three, two, one, or no red faces. Nets make icosahedron and dodecahedron models. The lesson asks how many faces meet at each vertex, a corner point. It also asks how many edges can be seen. Three-dimensional shapes can use straws, sticks, clay, or play dough.
keyPoints: Nisha joins 27 small cubes into a large solid cube.
Cubes are sorted by three, two, one, or no red faces.
Solid shapes can be built with straws, sticks, clay, or play dough.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects cube views, painting, nets, faces, and edges.

steps: Each vertex of a cube has 3 faces meeting at it.

activities.prompt: Explain why the regular pentagon tiles cannot make a completely covered display, while the equilateral triangle tiles can.
activities.answer: Regular pentagons cannot fill a region without leaving gaps, so they cannot make a completely covered display. Equilateral triangles tessellate: when fitted around a point, they leave no gaps and do not overlap. This makes their arrangement able to cover the display.

activities.context: At a school fair, thirty-five prizes are shared among seven tables. Each table receives five prizes. A helper checks the arrangement using the multiplication fact five times seven equals thirty-five. If the prizes are regrouped, the helper can use thirty-five divided by five to find the number of groups, or thirty-five divided by seven to find the size of each group.
activities.prompt: If the prizes are regrouped into five tables, how many prizes would each table receive?
options: Each table would receive seven prizes.
Each table would receive five prizes.
Each table would receive the whole set of prizes.
An equal share could not be made.

Five is the new number of groups.
why.Each table would receive the whole set o: Seven is the number of prizes in each group.
Dividing thirty-five equally into five groups works.

activities.explanation: Thirty-five divided by five equals seven.

activities.context: At a school fair, thirty-five prizes are shared among seven tables. Each table receives five prizes. A helper checks the arrangement using the multiplication fact five times seven equals thirty-five. If the prizes are regrouped, the helper can use thirty-five divided by five to find the number of groups, or thirty-five divided by seven to find the size of each group.
activities.prompt: If the helper divides thirty-five by five to check the regrouping, what should the helper conclude?
options: Each group would contain five prizes.
The prizes would form thirty-five groups.

The divisor is five, not the quotient.
Five describes the original size of each group.
why.The prizes would form thirty-five groups: Thirty-five is the dividend, not the number of groups.

activities.explanation: The quotient is seven.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the two related division facts?
activities.answer: The two division facts use the same dividend, thirty-five, but choose different divisors. Dividing by five gives seven, while dividing by seven gives five. Each fact answers a different question: one finds the size of each group, and the other finds the number of groups.
points: Both facts use thirty-five as the dividend.
One division uses five as the divisor.
The other division uses seven as the divisor.
The quotients answer different questions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school packs 1,248 counters into 6 equal boxes. A student checks the packing by splitting 1,248 into 1,200 and 48, then dividing each part by 6. Another student sorts 128 counters into 4 equal groups by halving twice. A different stack contains 1,992 counters, which must be divided into 4 equal groups.
activities.prompt: How many counters should be in each of the 6 equal boxes?

why.200: 200 ignores the 48 counters that were also divided.
why.8: 8 is only the result of dividing 48 by 6.
why.48: 48 is the smaller part, not the amount in each box.

activities.explanation: 208 is 200 + 8, so it includes both parts of 1,248.

activities.context: A school packs 1,248 counters into 6 equal boxes. A student checks the packing by splitting 1,248 into 1,200 and 48, then dividing each part by 6. Another student sorts 128 counters into 4 equal groups by halving twice. A different stack contains 1,992 counters, which must be divided into 4 equal groups.
activities.prompt: Which sequence shows the student's two halving steps for the 128 counters?

why.64 → 128 → 32: The first step reverses the given halving from 128 to 64.
why.128 → 32 → 64: The order swaps the second and first halving results.
why.32 → 64 → 128: The sequence starts with the final result and reverses the process.

activities.explanation: 128 becomes 64 after one halving and 32 after the second.

activities.prompt: Explain why splitting 1,248 into 1,200 and 48 helps to divide 1,248 by 6.
activities.answer: Split 1,248 into 1,200 and 48. Dividing 1,200 by 6 gives 200, and dividing 48 by 6 gives 8. Adding these two answers gives 208, so each of the 6 equal boxes has 208 counters.
points: Splits 1,248 into 1,200 and 48.
Divides each part by 6.
Finds 200 and 8.
Adds the answers to get 208.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Susie and Sunitha have a large coconut farm. They harvested 1,117 coconuts in April and sold 582 equally to 6 regular customers. Each customer gets 97 coconuts and will likely get less than 100. After the sales, 535 coconuts remain. Each bag holds 25 coconuts. Three bags hold 75 coconuts, and another bag is needed for the remainder. They need 22 bags altogether, and each person will get 4 bags.
activities.prompt: The farm must pack all 535 coconuts left after the sale. Which packing plan follows the rule for filling bags correctly?
options: Pack all 535 coconuts in 22 bags, with one bag partly filled.
Pack only the coconuts that exactly fill full bags and leave the remainder unpacked.
Put 25 coconuts in every bag, even if there are not enough coconuts.
Use fewer than 22 bags because dividing 535 by 25 appears to be exact.

why.Pack only the coconuts that exactly fill: This leaves some coconuts outside the bags.
why.Put 25 coconuts in every bag, even if th: This ignores the actual number of coconuts available.
why.Use fewer than 22 bags because dividing: The division has a remainder, so an extra bag is required.

activities.explanation: This packs every remaining coconut and includes a bag for the remainder.

activities.context: Susie and Sunitha have a large coconut farm. They harvested 1,117 coconuts in April and sold 582 equally to 6 regular customers. Each customer gets 97 coconuts and will likely get less than 100. After the sales, 535 coconuts remain. Each bag holds 25 coconuts. Three bags hold 75 coconuts, and another bag is needed for the remainder. They need 22 bags altogether, and each person will get 4 bags.
activities.prompt: Each person will get 4 bags. How should this plan be counted with the 22 bags needed for all the remaining coconuts?
options: Treat the two people's 4-bag portions as part of the 22-bag total.
Add 4 more bags for each person after preparing the 22 bags.
Prepare 22 bags for each person instead of sharing one total.
Count only one person's 4 bags and ignore the other person's portion.

why.Add 4 more bags for each person after pr: This treats the allocated bags as extras rather than part of the total.
why.Prepare 22 bags for each person instead: This incorrectly multiplies the number of bags needed.
why.Count only one person's 4 bags and ignor: This fails to account for both people's allocations.

activities.explanation: The two allocations come from the same total of 22 bags.

activities.context: Susie and Sunitha have a large coconut farm. They harvested 1,117 coconuts in April and sold 582 equally to 6 regular customers. Each customer gets 97 coconuts and will likely get less than 100. After the sales, 535 coconuts remain. Each bag holds 25 coconuts. Three bags hold 75 coconuts, and another bag is needed for the remainder. They need 22 bags altogether, and each person will get 4 bags.
activities.prompt: Which check confirms that the sale to the regular customers was shared equally?
options: Ensure that all 6 customers have identical totals.
Give one customer 97 coconuts while the others receive different totals.
Give each customer 25 coconuts because that is the capacity of one bag.
Give each customer 75 coconuts because that is the capacity of three bags.

why.Give one customer 97 coconuts while the: This gives the customers different totals.
why.Give each customer 25 coconuts because t: This confuses bag capacity with each customer's share.
why.Give each customer 75 coconuts because t: This confuses the capacity of three bags with each customer's share.

activities.explanation: Equal sharing means that every customer receives the same total.

activities.prompt: Explain why 22 bags are needed for the 535 coconuts remaining after the sale.
activities.answer: Dividing 535 by 25 shows how many complete bag-loads fit. The remaining coconuts do not fit in a full bag, so the farm needs one extra bag. Therefore, 22 bags are enough to hold every coconut left after the sale.
points: 535 coconuts must be packed.
Each bag holds 25 coconuts.
The remainder needs another bag.
The total required is 22 bags.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a farm, the manager divides 4,376 coconuts by 8 to find the yearly oil amount. Oil sells for ₹175 per litre. In May, husk earnings reached ₹9913 at ₹23 per kilogram. Coconut husk is used for making coir, a natural fibre used in gardening, farming, boat making and decorative items. Tender coconuts sell for ₹35 in hot summer months. For place-value practice, three Hundreds divided by 3 gives 1 Hundred.
activities.prompt: The farm uses the division method shown. What oil amount should be recorded for the year?

why.4,376 litres: This keeps the original coconut count instead of dividing it.
why.431 litres: This uses the amount of husk sold in May.
why.23 litres: This uses the husk price as though it were an oil amount.

activities.explanation: Correct: 4,376 divided by 8 equals 547.

activities.context: At a farm, the manager divides 4,376 coconuts by 8 to find the yearly oil amount. Oil sells for ₹175 per litre. In May, husk earnings reached ₹9913 at ₹23 per kilogram. Coconut husk is used for making coir, a natural fibre used in gardening, farming, boat making and decorative items. Tender coconuts sell for ₹35 in hot summer months. For place-value practice, three Hundreds divided by 3 gives 1 Hundred.
activities.prompt: After 3 Hundreds are divided by 3, what should the student do to show the result using Tens?
options: Write 3 Tens because the divisor was 3.
Keep 1 Hundred and also count 3 Ones.
Write 10 Hundreds because 10 is the new group size.

The divisor does not become the new quantity of Tens.
The division leaves 1 Hundred, not an extra group of Ones.
why.Write 10 Hundreds because 10 is the new: Regrouping changes how the amount is shown, not into 10 Hundreds.

activities.explanation: Correct: 1 Hundred can be regrouped as 10 Tens.

activities.prompt: Explain why dividing 4,376 by 8 gives the yearly oil amount and how this is connected with the selling price.
activities.answer: The farm divides the 4,376 coconuts by 8 because 8 coconuts are needed for 1 litre of oil. The division gives 547 litres. This is the oil amount for the year, and each litre sells for ₹175.
points: The farm has 4,376 coconuts.
Eight coconuts produce 1 litre of oil.
Dividing 4,376 by 8 gives 547 litres.
Each litre of oil sells for ₹175.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why 8 × 9 = 70 + 2 is a true mathematical statement.
activities.answer: The equals sign joins the two sides being compared. In 8 × 9 = 70 + 2, the left side and the right side have equal values. Therefore, the statement is true because the values on both sides match.
points: Identifies the equals sign as joining two sides.
Checks the values of both sides.
Explains that equal values make the statement true.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.title: Coconuts for Customers
activities.prompt: The farm sold 582 coconuts equally to 6 regular customers. How many did each customer get?
activities.explanation: Each customer gets 97 coconuts. Great sharing!

activities.title: Find the Dividend
activities.prompt: In 35 ÷ 5 = 7, which number is the dividend?
activities.explanation: The dividend is the number being divided. Here, it is 35.

activities.title: Bags for Everyone
activities.prompt: Each person will get 5 bags.
activities.explanation: Each person will get 4 bags. Keep checking!

activities.title: The Bag Count
activities.prompt: They need 22 bags altogether.
activities.explanation: Yes, 535 ÷ 25 shows that they need 22 bags altogether.

activities.title: Bag Capacity
activities.prompt: Each bag can hold ______ coconuts.
activities.hint: Think about the number of coconuts in one bag.
activities.explanation: Each bag can hold 25 coconuts. Well spotted!

activities.title: Halve Again
activities.prompt: Half of 64 is ______.
activities.hint: Halving means dividing by 2.
activities.explanation: Half of 64 is 32. This is the second halving step.

activities.title: Match the Amounts
activities.prompt: Match each item to its price or total.
activities.explanation: You matched each item with the correct amount from the lesson.

activities.title: Packing the Coconuts
activities.prompt: Put the coconut-bag steps in order.
items: The number of coconuts left is 535.
Find the number of bags by dividing 535 by 25.
activities.explanation: Start with 535 coconuts, divide by 25, then find 22 bags. Nice work!
